title: Built an AI research desk for Kalshi that can't place a trade unless I click approve (demo money, 3 days in)
author: Difficult_Low_8618
selftext:
I have been messing with Kalshi's demo exchange the last few days and ended up building a local dashboard for it. runs on my laptop and just talks to the Kalshi API.

It pulls every open market and puts stuff next to it that Kalshi doesn't show, like sportsbook lines, live scores, weather forecasts. then Claude (or Gemini, I can switch) researches a market and proposes a trade with its reasoning. I have to approve every one. there are small hard caps on order size and daily spend, plus a kill switch the AI can't touch.

The part I care most about is that I assume the market price is mostly right. every AI estimate gets blended back toward the market price before anything happens, and the model only gets more weight once its raw guesses actually beat the market over enough settled calls. it hasn't earned anything yet. a second model also gives a quick independent number, and if the two disagree by a large margin, it sizes the bet down.

The parts that broke(and a lot did):

* ESPN was rejecting every request for a day, so my "live scores and lines" never showed anything and I didn't notice until I checked the logs
* Kalshi keeps your balance per shard (baseball is on a different one than most things), so my first order failed with "insufficient shard balance"
* my P&L was ignoring fees, for now

The results I have so far: 2 settled, both wins, which means nothing. the demo books are super thin too. in my paper sim, a strategy that buys when sportsbooks disagree with Kalshi only filled a small fraction of what it wanted, so I don't trust demo results to say much about live.

The ai agent is not going live until it can repeatedly beat the market price in at least one category. If you have built something like this, how do you deal with thin books? 

And for anyone running something similar: how much edge do you need before a trade is worth it after fees and spread?

Another question I have is what outside data has been actually useful for you? I'm pulling sportsbook lines and weather forecasts, and wondering what else to add"

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
For thin books, I’d treat edge as a capacity curve rather than one number. Replay the sportsbook-disagreement strategy against timestamped Kalshi order-book snapshots, consume only displayed size at each level, and report expected value by requested stake. A 6-point discrepancy might support $5 but disappear by $50 once spread and depth are included.

Set the trade threshold from the fill-weighted price, current fee schedule, and an uncertainty buffer for the model estimate. I’d also make missing ESPN data force an explicit “unavailable” state, since silently absent live scores could otherwise look like evidence. Does the demo API expose enough depth history to reconstruct partial fills and queue position?

replies.author: Difficult_Low_8618
replies.body:
Thanks, this is very helpful. My paper sim takes a share of visible depth, charges the fee, and re-reads the book after a short delay, so I get fill rate and slippage per strategy. I don't report EV by stake size though, and that's probably the biggest gap.

The threshold is pretty much a fixed edge number, a bit stricter in categories where the model's been wrong. closest thing to an uncertainty buffer is blending toward the market price and sizing down when the two models disagree. A threshold built from fill price + fees + a buffer sounds way better, I'll try that!

ESPN is a fair point. Right now when the pull fails, the card just loses the number and logs it, so yeah, silent absence. I'll make it say "unavailable."

As far as depth history, Kalshi's docs only seem to show the current book over REST, and the historical stuff covers trades, candlesticks and orders, not depth. There's a queue position endpoint for your own orders and a websocket with snapshot + deltas I could log, but I haven't checked if demo supports it. If not I'll start saving my own snapshots.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
pulling every estimate back toward the market price is the sane starting point, most of these projects skip it and the model's confidence gets read as edge.

the bit I'd watch is what counts as enough settled calls. markets on the same game or the same weather day settle together, so twenty calls can really be three or four independent ones, and the model can look calibrated off one lucky cluster.

for stocks I built something on a similar loop, Quantradin, at quantradin.com. an agent proposes on paper and you watch whether it ever earns more weight. free, no real money involved.

replies.author: Difficult_Low_8618
replies.body: That is a good point, that's a real hole. The 30 is just a count of settled calls as far as I know, so a few markets on the same game or the same weather day would count as separate samples. I should probably count by event or by day instead, or at least show both numbers. Thanks for flagging that issue!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: showing both is the honest version. if the by-day number is way lower, that tells you more than any calibration chart will

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Shrinking the model's estimate toward the market price and only giving it weight once it beats the market is a sound design, and so is the kill switch the AI can't touch. For how much edge you need, a rough rule is that your edge has to exceed the fee plus about half the spread, and you should measure it with a Brier score on settled calls before going live. On thin books, I'd record fill rate and treat missed fills as a cost. For outside data, economics markets (CPI, Fed, jobs) have known release times, and Cymetica's EventTrader is one source of event timing for them.

comments.author: Alternative-Song2025
comments.body: blending every estimate back toward the market price is the part most people skip, that's the right instinct. the thing that bit me was demo fills. sim handed me the price i asked for, live i was crossing 2 to 3 cents of spread and that ate most of what the model thought it had. also time your approve click, on the short markets the quote has usually moved by then.
